title: Two Decades Later, 'Superman Returns' Still Defies Easy Labels
summary: It's a contested field, but John Williams' majestic 'Superman' theme is arguably one of the greatest pieces of film music ever composed. Almost five decades on, that stirring orchestral march remains synonymous with Krypton's most famous son—still capable of making grown adults want to dash out of phone booths while ripping open their shirts. So it's perhaps not surprising that director Bryan Singer couldn't imagine using any other music when he signed on to helm 'Superman Returns,' which celebrates its 20th anniversary this weekend. 'From day one, Bryan said he wouldn't even greenlight the movie if he couldn't use the John Williams music,' composer John Ottman revealed. 'That's how important it was to Bryan. I had moments of wanting to evolve the theme a little bit and alter it slightly, but Bryan was against any modifications at all, even down to the last flute flourish.' That devotion to Richard Donner's 1978 classic 'Superman: The Movie' stretched far beyond the score. 'Superman Returns' is an unashamed love letter to the film that made us believe a man could fly. Yet it's also a movie of contradictions. While technically a continuation of the Christopher Reeve series, it's simultaneously a reboot. The filmmakers conveniently pretended that the disappointing 'Superman III' and 'Superman IV' never happened, picking up the story five years after 'Superman II.' But instead of being set in 1985, the film takes place in 2006 with an entirely new cast. The plot sees Superman returning from a years-long journey to the remains of Krypton, only to find that Lois Lane has moved on—she's now in a relationship, has a young son, and has written a Pulitzer Prize-winning article titled 'Why the world doesn't need Superman.' Meanwhile, Lex Luthor emerges from retirement with a dastardly real estate scheme involving Kryptonian technology to build a new continent. Singer opted to cast an unknown as Superman, just as Donner had done with the peerless Christopher Reeve. Brandon Routh makes a decent Man of Steel—heroic yet touchingly melancholic—but his Clark Kent is underwritten. Kate Bosworth's Lois lacks the screwball energy of Margot Kidder's performance, and Kevin Spacey's Lex Luthor feels overly vicious compared to Gene Hackman's charmingly timeless version. Even before release, the film attracted controversy: the darker red cape and smaller 'S' shield, eschewing the primary colors of the Reeve era for a more muted, 'realistic' superhero aesthetic. Two decades on, 'Superman Returns' remains a fascinating artifact—a film caught between honoring the past and launching a new future, much like the character it celebrates.
why_it_matters: How filmmakers handle beloved characters can shape entire franchises for years; this film shows the tough balance between nostalgia and innovation, which impacts how studios approach reboots and why audiences connect with stories.

background_read: Superman first appeared in comic books in 1938 and quickly became one of the most iconic superheroes, later adapted into radio shows, TV series, and films. The 1978 movie 'Superman: The Movie,' directed by Richard Donner (known for 'The Goonies' and 'Lethal Weapon'), set a high bar with Christopher Reeve's performance and John Williams' score. After that film's success, three sequels followed, but the third and fourth were widely panned by critics and audiences.

In the early 2000s, superhero movies like 'X-Men' (directed by Bryan Singer) and 'Spider-Man' revived the genre, leading Warner Bros. to attempt a new Superman film. After several canceled projects, Singer was hired to direct 'Superman Returns' in 2006. His decision to model the film as a direct sequel to 'Superman II'—while ignoring the later sequels—was an unusual choice known as a 'soft reboot.' This meant the movie existed in a strange timeline, acknowledging the earlier story but with a 20-year gap and new actors.

The film arrived during a transition period: superhero movies were becoming darker and more 'realistic,' as seen in Christopher Nolan's 'Batman Begins' (2005). 'Superman Returns' tried to balance old-fashioned hopefulness with a more muted, serious tone, which contributed to its mixed reception. Two decades later, it's remembered as an ambitious but flawed tribute that struggled to please both nostalgic fans and modern audiences.

perspectives.description: Devoted fans appreciated the film's deep reverence for the original 1978 movie. Using John Williams' score and echoing Donner's style created emotional continuity and honored the character's cinematic legacy, making longtime Superman lovers feel seen.

Critics argued that the film was trapped by its own nostalgia, failing to offer a fresh vision. By copying so much from the past—music, plot beats, even casting an unknown—it didn't take enough risks, leaving the characters underdeveloped and the story forgettable compared to bolder superhero films emerging at the time.

From a neutral viewpoint, 'Superman Returns' reflects the mid-2000s tension in Hollywood between established franchises and a changing audience. It arrived just before the Marvel Cinematic Universe revolutionized interconnected storytelling, and its mixed reception reveals how difficult it is to revive a classic hero without losing what made him work in a new era.

Looking forward, the film's failure to generate a sequel led to a complete reset with 2013's 'Man of Steel,' a grittier take. This pivot influenced all later DC films. The Superman Returns experiment raises enduring questions: can a traditional, optimistic Superman survive in a market that craves darker antiheroes, or must the character evolve?
